text:
Apollo 13: The Mission That Came Home

On the afternoon of April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center in Florida carrying three men toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, was a veteran of three earlier flights and was making his fourth trip into space. Fred Haise, the lunar module pilot, was a rookie. The third seat belonged to Jack Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before. Ken Mattingly, the original command module pilot, had been exposed to German measles, and NASA decided to replace him rather than risk illness in flight. Swigert trained hard in the short time available, and the crew was declared ready.

The plan was ambitious but familiar by then. Apollo 11 had landed in 1969, and Apollo 12 had followed that November. Apollo 13 was to touch down in the hilly Fra Mauro region and bring back rocks from highlands the earlier crews had not visited. The crew named their command module Odyssey. The lunar module, the spindly craft meant to carry two of them down to the surface, was called Aquarius.

The launch had a small warning in it. During the climb, the center engine of the second stage shut down early, and the remaining engines burned longer to make up the difference. The spacecraft reached its planned path. For two days the flight was so smooth that flight controllers in Houston joked about how little there was to do. A television broadcast from the ship, intended for the public, drew little attention from the networks.

The trouble began on the evening of April 13, nearly fifty-six hours into the flight. The spacecraft was about two hundred thousand miles from Earth. Mission Control asked Swigert to switch on the stirring fans in the supercold oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module, which keep the contents from settling into layers. Swigert flipped the switch. Moments later there was a bang, and the ship shuddered. Warning lights lit up. Swigert said, Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here. Lovell repeated it a moment later, and the sentence entered history in the slightly altered form that people remember.

What had happened took days to piece together. Oxygen tank number two had been damaged years earlier on the ground, when it was dropped a short distance during handling. Later, during a test, its heaters ran far too long because a switch had been built for a lower voltage than the ground equipment supplied. The heat cooked the Teflon insulation on the wiring inside, leaving bare copper. When Swigert turned on the fans, a spark in that tank ignited the damaged insulation. The tank burst, and the blast tore off a panel of the service module and crippled the neighboring tank.

The loss was cruel in its arithmetic. The command module Odyssey drew its electricity and its drinking water from fuel cells that ran on the oxygen and hydrogen now venting into space. Within hours the main power would be gone. Haise looked out a window and saw gas streaming away from the ship. Lovell, glancing at it, understood that the Moon was no longer possible. The question now was whether they could get home at all.

Flight director Gene Kranz and his teams in Houston turned to an idea that had been studied but never tried in earnest. The lunar module was a complete little spacecraft with its own oxygen, power and engine, built to sustain two men for about two days. Now it would be a lifeboat for three men for four. The crew crowded into Aquarius, and Odyssey was shut down to save its small reserve of battery power for the final descent through the atmosphere.

Next came the matter of direction. The ship was on a path that would have swung it past the Moon and far out into space if nothing were done. Controllers weighed a quick turnaround against a longer loop around the Moon. The turnaround would have required the damaged service module engine, which no one trusted. Instead they chose to swing around the far side and use the lunar module's descent engine, a motor built for landing and never meant for this. A burn of that engine a couple of hours after the closest approach to the Moon sped the ship up and shortened the trip. As they rounded the Moon, the crew passed farther from Earth than any humans had been or have been since, nearly two hundred and fifty thousand miles. They took photographs and tried to keep their minds on the work.

Life aboard became a struggle against three enemies. The first was cold. With power conserved, the cabin temperature fell to a little above freezing, and condensation beaded on the walls. The crew slept little and wore whatever they had. The second was thirst. Water was rationed to a few ounces a day each, and Haise developed a fever and a painful infection that he kept largely to himself. The third was the air itself. Carbon dioxide exhaled by three men built up in a cabin designed for two, and the lithium hydroxide canisters that scrub it out were filling. The spare canisters in Odyssey were square, and the receptacles in Aquarius were round.

Engineers on the ground gathered the same materials the astronauts had on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, a sock, hoses from the spacesuits and a roll of duct tape. They built an adapter and read the instructions up to the crew, step by step. The men copied it, and the carbon dioxide reading dropped back into the safe range.

The rest of the trip was a string of careful decisions. A small course correction, made by hand without the usual guidance computer, depended on keeping the Earth steady in a window. The crew used the line between day and night on the planet as a reference and burned the engine for a timed interval. Meanwhile, back on Earth, Mattingly and a team of engineers in a simulator worked out a procedure to restart the sleeping command module with far less power than anyone had planned for. They tested it again and again until it fit within the limits of the batteries.

On April 17, the crew prepared for the end. Hours before entry, they jettisoned the damaged service module, and as it drifted away they saw for the first time how much had been destroyed. A whole side of it was missing. Then they climbed back into Odyssey, powered it up using the new procedure, and let go of Aquarius, which had served them better than anyone had a right to expect.

The last uncertainty was the blackout. During reentry, a spacecraft is wrapped in ionized gas that blocks radio for about three minutes. This time the silence stretched past that, and in Houston the room grew very quiet as the seconds ticked on. Controllers wondered about the heat shield, which no one could inspect. Then, after more than a minute beyond the expected time, Swigert's voice came through. Three parachutes bloomed over the Pacific near Samoa, and Odyssey settled into the water at about one in the afternoon, Houston time, under a clear sky.

The crew were exhausted, thinner and somewhat dehydrated, but alive and well. Navy helicopters carried them to the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. The mission was officially called a successful failure, since the Moon had not been reached but every life had been saved. A review board traced the cause to the tank, and engineers changed the design of future spacecraft so that such a failure could not be repeated. Apollo 13 remains the best remembered of the missions precisely because it did not go to plan, and because the people on the ground and in space refused to let it end in tragedy.
